newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO sees compromise on labour, farm rows - officials.
newsitem.headline: WTO sees compromise on labour, farm rows - officials.

text.p: World trade ministers agreed on Thursday on a final declaration to cap their inaugural meeting, with compromises reached on the contentious issues of labour standards and agriculture, officials said.

"We got everything," a beaming World Trade Organisation (WTO) Director-General Renato Ruggiero told Reuters as he began a late-night meeting with heads of delegations on the fourth day of the December 9-13 conference.

"The labour issue is in the final declaration," a senior negotiator said, referring to the contentious issue of whether to allow a mention of core labour standards that would link trade to improving workers' conditions.
Pakistani Commerce Minister Muhammad Zubair Khan, among the final hold-outs against any mention, confirmed that labour had been included.

Compromise had also been reached to include agriculture, thus ironing out the final contentious issues and paving the way for a declaration on Friday to crown the inaugural meeting of the WTO, which operates by consensus.

Diplomats said the declaration would have wording recognising the commitment of all WTO countries to core labour standards and recognising the Geneva-based International Labour Organisation (ILO) as the competent body to establish what those standards are.
The deal will say that WTO countries are opposed to the use of trade measures for protectionist purposes and have no wish to deprive low-wage countries of their competitive advantages.
The ministers will also say that the WTO and ILO will continue their existing collaboration in the area of labour, officials said.

"We are happy with what has come out," said Pakistan's Zubair Khan, adding that there would also be reference in the chairman's statement after the declaration was issued on Friday to say that labour standards were not a part of the WTO agenda.

Other officials said the final moves to an agreement came when the core group of holdouts found that they had little support left after Pakistan and Egypt decided to accept compromise wording in the declaration.
Diplomats said India and two other countries that they did not identify were the last to agree.
